Survey-Weighted Explainable Gradient Boosting for Regional Disparities in PHQ-9-Defined Depression in Korea: 2024 Korea Community Health Survey.
papers.abstract: To analyze regional disparities in depression defined by the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) among Korean adults using spatial statistics and survey-weighted prediction models based on the 2024 Korea Community Health Survey (KCHS), and to visualize region-specific contributing factors using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) METHODS: This cross-sectional secondary analysis evaluated 231,469 respondents. Survey weights were applied to logistic regression, XGBoost, and LightGBM models to classify concurrent depression status, operationally defined as a PHQ-9 score of 10 or higher. Spatial autocorrelation was assessed using global Moran's I and Local Indicators of Spatial Association. SHAP values quantified global feature importance and the spatial heterogeneity of dominant positive mean contributors across 250 harmonized municipal units RESULTS: The national weighted prevalence of PHQ-9-defined depression was 4.1 percent, with weak positive global spatial autocorrelation and regional variation ranging from 0.9 percent to 8.2 percent. In the independent test set, LightGBM achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.92, an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.43, and a Brier score of 0.03. No local association remained significant after false discovery rate correction. SHAP analysis identified perceived stress, subjective happiness, and subjective health status as the most influential global predictors. Mapping revealed spatial heterogeneity: perceived stress was the most frequent dominant positive mean contributor, whereas other municipal units showed subjective health status, subjective happiness, smoking status, sleep duration, income, and other contributors. Regional contributor rank retention varied across bootstrap samples (median, 72.5%). Psychosocial and structural characteristics contributed to concurrent classification of PHQ-9-defined depression, with exploratory geographic variation in aggregated SHAP contributions. Combining explainable machine learning with spatial statistics may inform further local assessment. This study was exempted from review by the Institutional Review Board of Kangbuk Samsung Hospital (KBSMC IRB No. 2026-02-008).

papers.title: The Hypothalamic Paraventricular Nucleus as an Integrative Hub of Circadian Regulation and a Therapeutic Target in Disease.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms are endogenous, approximately 24-hour oscillations that align physiology and behavior with the environmental light-dark cycle and support homeostasis. In mammals, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) serves as the central circadian pacemaker, but its neuronal projections are restricted to a relatively small set of hypothalamic targets. The hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus (PVN) is an important downstream integrative node that receives direct and indirect temporal signals from the SCN and integrates them with metabolic, visceral, stress-related, and limbic inputs. Through functionally distinct neuroendocrine, autonomic, and central-projecting neuronal populations, the PVN contributes to the temporal regulation of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activity, glucose metabolism, feeding behavior, nociceptive sensitivity, and cardiovascular function. Cell-type-specific genetic and transcriptomic studies further indicate that PVN neuronal populations exhibit distinct clock-related molecular programs. Studies predominantly in nocturnal rodent models have linked disruption of PVN clocks or rhythmic output to aging-associated decline, metabolic dysfunction, altered tumor immunity, neurodegenerative disease, and pain-related phenotypes. Human post-mortem studies have reported heterogeneous PVN changes in Alzheimer's disease, but direct evidence of PVN clock or SCN-PVN circuit dysfunction in humans remains limited. This review integrates circuit-, cellular-, and molecular-level evidence for the PVN's role in circadian regulation, evaluates interventions spanning timed drug delivery, meal timing, light exposure, and PVN-focused experimental manipulation, and outlines the challenges of translating preclinical findings into clinical practice.

papers.title: Beyond Classification Accuracy: Building Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence for Clinical Electroencephalography.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) remains important in clinical neuroscience because it records brain activity as a time-resolved physiological process. It offers millisecond temporal resolution, can be used at the bedside and supports prolonged monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded EEG analysis through automated pattern recognition, representation learning, large-scale screening and decision support in epilepsy, sleep medicine, cognitive disorders, psychiatric conditions, intensive care, disorders of consciousness and anaesthesia monitoring. High classification accuracy in a research dataset, however, is not clinical readiness. EEG signals are shaped by physiological state, artefacts, acquisition systems, preprocessing choices and clinical context. Labels may come from expert annotations, diagnostic categories, behavioural scales, treatment responses or long-term outcomes, and these sources do not always define the same biological target. This review argues that EEG-AI translation should be judged by the strength of its evidence, not by technical performance alone. We examine why EEG is valuable yet hard to standardize, how EEG features can serve as candidate biomarkers, and why translational maturity differs across clinical scenarios. We then discuss the evidence gaps behind high-performing models, focusing on target validity, data leakage, confounding, external validation and clinically aligned metrics. Finally, we argue for clinical understandability rather than model interpretability alone, and for human-machine workflows rather than isolated classifiers. Future EEG-AI systems should be assessed by whether their outputs are biologically plausible, externally generalizable, understandable to clinicians and safe in real-world care.

papers.title: State-Dependent EEG Markers of Excitation/Inhibition and Hemodynamic State Are Associated with Random Noise Stimulation Effects.
papers.abstract: Non-invasive brain stimulation effects vary substantially across individuals, yet the physiological factors associated with this variability remain unclear. We tested whether baseline and task-related EEG markers of excitation/inhibition (E/I) and hemodynamic state are associated with the effects of transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) on learning. Participants completed a mathematical learning task during active or sham tRNS. We indexed E/I-related population dynamics using the EEG aperiodic exponent, for which lower values have been linked to relatively greater excitation than inhibition, and assessed hemodynamic state using fNIRS-derived oxygenated hemoglobin (HbO). Behavioral learning was modeled using generalized linear mixed-effects models. tRNS accelerated learning relative to sham stimulation but did not reliably induce pre-post changes in resting-state aperiodic exponent or HbO. Instead, stimulation effects were state-dependent. Higher resting-state aperiodic exponent and lower resting-state HbO were associated with greater behavioral gains under tRNS, while task-related aperiodic exponent was associated with stimulation-related differences in learning. Task-evoked HbO was associated with learning rate but did not significantly differentiate stimulation effects. Across modalities, the findings identify complementary electrophysiological and hemodynamic correlates of variability in learning under stimulation. However, statistical support for the EEG moderation effects was attenuated in models including participant-specific learning slopes, indicating sensitivity to random-effects specification and the need for replication. The findings argue against a simple tonic-shift account of tRNS and support a state-dependent framework in which stimulation effects depend on ongoing electrophysiological and hemodynamic context. EEG and fNIRS provided complementary information about variability in learning and stimulation response, supporting multimodal approaches to understanding and individualizing neuromodulation.

papers.title: Objective assessment of depressive symptoms using eye-tracking features: An exploratory pilot study.
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) exhibits significant symptom heterogeneity, challenging precise clinical assessment. Current evaluations rely on subjective patient and clinician reports, limiting objective monitoring. Eye-tracking technology offers a non-invasive approach to assessing and characterizing clinical features in depressive patients, enabling personalized assessment and management. This cross-sectional pilot study included 74 patients with MDD and 80 healthy controls. Participants completed a free-viewing task and a visual search task. Depressive, anxiety (including tension), anhedonia and sleep symptoms were assessed using the HAMD-17, HAMA, DARS, and PSQI scales. Correlations between symptom scores and eye-tracking variables were analyzed in an exploratory, hypothesis-generating framework, followed by regression models to identify associated eye-tracking variables. Multiple eye-tracking features showed exploratory associations with specific symptoms, although none of these associations survived correction for multiple comparisons. Suicidal ideation was associated with longer average fixation duration for threatening pictures during the free-viewing task (AUC 0.753); anhedonia severity with first fixation latency/duration for angry faces in the visual search task; sleep disturbance with longer fixation durations and first fixation latency for positive faces; and tension with longer first fixation duration for negative faces (AUC 0.743). Specific eye-tracking features, particularly those related to processing threatening pictures and emotional faces, were associated with severity of depressive symptoms such as suicidal ideation, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, and tension in this exploratory pilot study. These preliminary findings require replication in independent samples before clinical application but support the potential utility of eye-tracking as an objective tool for assessing symptom domains in MDD.

papers.title: Individualized Transcranial Temporal Interference Stimulation (TIS): Research Advancements and Clinical Translation Pathways.
papers.abstract: Transcranial temporal interference stimulation (TIS) is a promising tool for non-invasive deep brain modulation, yet inter-individual anatomical differences cause substantial electric field (E-field) variability under identical parameters, hindering clinical translation. We review recent progress (2017-2026) in individualized TIS, focusing on why inter-individual variability occurs and how to address it for clinical applications. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, preprint repositories (bioRxiv, medRxiv, arXiv), and clinical trial registries from June 2017 through August 2026, synthesizing studies across quantitative E-field variability, biophysical mediation mechanisms, computational optimization frameworks, and human trials. Even with individualized optimization, the focal spot can shift by up to 1.2cm between subjects. Target modulation depth varies with age and sex, largely due to variations in skull thickness and cerebrospinal fluid volume. For E-field optimization, individualized finite element method (FEM) modeling remains the most accurate approach, whereas faster population-based optimization (17% error margin) is viable only for superficial brain areas. In human translational studies, a clear distinction must be maintained across levels of evidence: while individualized montages targeting the striatum and subthalamic nucleus demonstrate physiological target engagement, behavioral modulation in healthy cohorts, and preliminary acute symptom relief in pilot patient trials, definitive clinical efficacy in large-scale randomized trials (e.g., ongoing nucleus accumbens protocols) and effective active sham protocols remain ongoing challenges. Individualized planning is essential for deep TIS. Future studies should focus on multi-center trials and standardized in vivo closed-loop validation using functional neuroimaging and electrophysiology.

papers.title: [Sleep reimagined: Current developments in sleep medicine for everyday medical practice].
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders are among the most common complaints in medical practice. Regardless of their field of expertise and level of care, patients report non-restorative sleep, difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep, daytime fatigue or concentration problems. Nevertheless, sleep problems are often only casually recorded in everyday clinical practice or interpreted as a concomitant symptom of other diseases. Sleep is not a non-specific characteristic of well-being, but an actively regulated biological functional state with high clinical significance.Sleep influences central bodily functions such as cardiovascular regulation, metabolism, immune response and neural processing. Changes in these systems almost always affect sleep. Conversely, persistent sleep disorders can contribute to the manifestation or progression of chronic diseases. This results in a paradigm shift in medical practice: sleep should not only be addressed when symptoms are pronounced but should be understood as a regular component of the medical history.

papers.title: [Sleep Medicine in ENT Practice - An Overview of Diagnosis and Current Treatment].
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for health and quality of life. In the field of otorhinolaryngology (ENT), sleep medicine has become an integral part of patient care, particularly in the management of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). With an increasing prevalence of sleep disorders, especially in the German population, and their association with various comorbid conditions, modern therapeutic approaches are crucial. This overview provides a practical summary of diagnostic methods and current treatment options available for sleep-related breathing disorders. Diagnosing OSA typically involves a structured, stepwise approach, beginning with a comprehensive medical history and validated questionnaires, followed by ambulatory polygraphy, and in some cases, polysomnography (PSG) in sleep laboratories. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) and the International Classification of Sleep Disorders (ICSD-3) provide standards for diagnosing and classifying sleep disorders, including sleep-related breathing disorders like OSA. Prevalence rates indicate that about 30% of men and 13% of women develop OSA in their lifetime. Risk factors include age, obesity, genetic predisposition, and anatomical variations in the upper airway. Effective treatment for OSA includes conservative measures like weight loss and continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy, as well as surgical options such as tonsillectomy, uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP), and, in severe cases, hypoglossal nerve stimulation. CPAP therapy remains the gold standard, especially for moderate to severe OSA, offering significant improvement in daytime sleepiness and cardiovascular comorbidities. The diagnostic process involves a combination of clinical evaluation, validated screening tools like the STOP-BANG questionnaire, and polygraphic or PSG assessments. Treatment aims to reduce apneic episodes, improve sleep architecture, and enhance quality of life. In patients who cannot tolerate CPAP or prefer less invasive options, mandibular advancement devices or positional therapy may be recommended. Surgical interventions are considered when anatomical factors significantly contribute to OSA. Unaddressed OSA is associated with severe health risks, including cardiovascular diseases and impaired cognitive function, and it poses safety concerns, particularly for drivers and operators of heavy machinery. Therefore, timely diagnosis and individualized treatment are essential for improving both health outcomes and quality of life in affected individuals.

papers.title: Sleep: And then there was light!
papers.abstract: How has access to electricity impacted sleep in rural or urban environments? New research shows that electricity in previously unexposed communities delays and reduces sleep duration by about an hour in rural communities, but only delays sleep in urban communities.

papers.title: Involvement of JAK2/STAT3, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and M1/M2 microglial polarization in the possible effects of baricitinib for mitigating reserpine-induced fibromyalgia in rats.
papers.abstract: Fibromyalgia (FM) is a chronic pain disorder characterized by widespread musculoskeletal pain accompanied by fatigue, mood disturbances, and sleep abnormalities. Baricitinib, a selective Janus kinase (JAK) 1/2 inhibitor, has potent anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects and is approved for various resistant inflammatory conditions. The present study aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential of baricitinib against fibromyalgia-like manifestations induced by reserpine in rats. Reserpine (1 mg/kg/day, subcutaneous) was administered for three consecutive days to induce FM-like pathology, followed by oral treatment with baricitinib at low and high doses for 14 consecutive days. Reserpine administration resulted in marked neuroinflammatory changes, evidenced by elevated levels of interleukin-1β, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-α, along with increased phosphorylation of JAK2, STAT3, PI3K, AKT, and mTOR signaling proteins. Baricitinib treatment significantly ameliorated these molecular alterations and attenuated histopathological damage in the spinal cord. Furthermore, baricitinib partially restored dopamine D2 receptor levels and modulated M1/M2-associated microglial markers, as indicated by reduced CD86 expression and enhanced CD163 immunoreactivity. Additionally, behavioral assessments demonstrated significant improvements in pain sensitivity, locomotor activity, and depressive-like symptoms. These findings highlight the neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects of baricitinib in a reserpine-induced fibromyalgia model and support its potential role in targeting neuroimmune mechanisms underlying fibromyalgia.

papers.title: Neural and behavioral signatures of live and video demonstrations in bimanual interpersonal coordination: An EEG and kinematic study.
papers.abstract: Neural oscillations in the mu (8-12 Hz) and high-beta (21-30 Hz) bands are established markers of interpersonal coordination. However, the influence of social context-live versus video modeling - on sensorimotor engagement during coordinated action remains poorly understood. This study investigated how model type and engagement mode (execution vs. observation) shape neural and behavioral responses during an interpersonal motor coordination task. Twenty right-handed females (25.47 ± 3.4 years) were randomly assigned to train with either a live or video model (n = 10 per group). The same model performed 30-s sequences of elbow flexion-extension. Participants observed and executed the task with both live and video models across three phases (pre-test, post-test, and retention). During practice following the pre-test, participants trained coordinately with the model for 30 min. EEG activity was recorded from C3, Cz, and C4 electrodes, and spectral power was analyzed in the mu (8-12 Hz) and high-beta (21-30 Hz) bands. Kinematic coordination was quantified using vector coding of coupling angles between the participant and the model during execution. Results indicated significant desynchronization in both mu and high-beta bands during execution trials. Compared with the video-model condition, live-model interaction produced stronger high-beta suppression and more stable kinematic coupling. Additionally, mu suppression during observation increased across practice phases from pre-test to post-test and retention. Social context shapes interpersonal synchronization; physical presence may enhance perception-action coupling and predictive motor coding underlying joint action.

papers.title: Changes in P300 neural correlates during voice-pitch discrimination under conditions supporting F0-based auditory segregation.
papers.abstract: Previous event-related potential (ERP) studies have examined effects of tone frequency, level, and duration on P300 amplitude and latency during two-tone frequency discrimination using the oddball paradigm. However, these studies have focused outside voice-pitch frequency range, where fundamental frequency (F0) differences are critical for auditory scene segregation. The current study investigates how F0 differences and moderate tone levels influence P300 amplitude and latency during two-tone F0 discrimination. Younger adults with normal hearing heard standard and deviant tones in oddball paradigm. The standard tone had an F0 of 100 Hz, while deviant tone had F0s of 103, 106, 126, and 179 Hz, corresponding to F0 differences of 3, 6, 26, and 79 Hz. Tones were 400 ms duration and presented at 65 or 75 dB SPL. F0 difference and duration were selected to ensure reliable F0 discrimination and segregation. P300 responses were examined by analyzing ERPs for standard and deviant trials. Mean parietal P300 amplitudes were significantly higher from 6 Hz to 26 Hz and 26 Hz to 79 Hz at both levels, whereas mean parietal P300 latencies were significantly shorter at 79 Hz than at 26 Hz. Higher behavioral discrimination performance (d') was significantly related to stronger mean parietal P300 amplitudes but not to shorter mean parietal P300 latencies. These findings suggest that P300 amplitude provides a more informative index of the neural processing underlying two-tone voice-pitch discrimination when F0-based segregation cues are available.

papers.title: Neuropeptide signaling in perioperative neurocognitive disorders: Receptor biology, mechanistic links, and a cautious prevention framework.
papers.abstract: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND) encompass postoperative delirium, delayed neurocognitive recovery, and postoperative neurocognitive disorder in patients with a vulnerable brain. Neuropeptides provide a receptor-defined signaling layer that can couple tissue injury, nociception, arousal, sleep, vascular regulation, and glial responses. This review integrates clinical and translational evidence for substance P/neurokinin-1, neuropeptide Y/Y receptors, orexin-A/orexin receptors, and vasoactive intestinal peptide/pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide pathways within the broader biology of PND. Current human evidence is strongest for perioperative risk factors, delirium phenotyping, and selected preventive bundles; direct evidence that neuropeptide pathways cause or predict PND remains limited. We therefore distinguish established associations from preclinical mechanisms and hypothesis-generating therapeutic opportunities. The proposed framework links preoperative brain-reserve assessment and medication optimization with intraoperative protection of neurovascular and circuit function and postoperative restoration of sleep, mobility, and orientation. Biomarkers and neuropeptide signatures may enrich future trials, but no validated thresholds or individual-level neuropeptide-guided treatment pathway is currently available. Progress will require receptor-resolved assays, longitudinal human sampling, external validation, and pragmatic trials that test clinical utility rather than mechanistic plausibility alone.

papers.title: Sotalol and flecainide dual therapy in a dog with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
papers.abstract: A four-year-old Doberman pinscher was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation (AF) and equivocal dilated cardiomyopathy phenotype. Electrical cardioversion (ECV) was performed following two weeks of amiodarone treatment; however, the dog developed recurrent AF within one week post ECV. Following two additional months of amiodarone therapy, the dog represented with sinus rhythm and new hepatopathy. In-hospital electrocardiographic monitoring identified paroxysmal AF during sleep. Amiodarone therapy was transitioned to sotalol therapy, which prevented further paroxysmal AF episodes. However, episodes of atypical AFL were frequently observed during sleep at follow-ups over five months. Flecainide was added to the sotalol therapy, and no further occurrence of AF or AFL was observed at follow-ups over 10 months. This report highlights that dogs may present with paroxysmal AF post ECV. When the paroxysmal AF is likely vagally mediated, sotalol and flecainide dual therapy may be effective in preventing further occurrence of AF and AFL.

papers.title: Dynamic red-blue lighting is associated with diurnal clock-gene expression and photosynthetic responses in pak choi.
papers.abstract: Light supplies energy for photosynthesis, while its spectral composition also acts as an environmental signal. significantly enhanced oscillatory robustness. However, how light quality is associated with coordinated changes in circadian regulation and photosynthetic responses remains insufficiently understood. In this study, pak choi was used as the experimental material to establish a coupled analytical framework linking light-quality input, core circadian components comprising CCA1/LHY, PRR9/PRR7, PRR5/TOC1, and ELF4/LUX, and photosynthetic responses.Relative to the white-light reference, the tested continuous red-light regime showed later fitted peak times of core clock genes, whereas the blue-light regime showed earlier phases. These differences were observed under unequal source PPFDs and treatment DLIs. In contrast, red-blue combined light, particularly dynamic intermittent red-blue supplementation, significantly enhanced oscillatory robustness and maintained a circadian pattern closer to that under white light. Among the photosynthesis-related genes examined, BcLhcb1 showed a pronounced response to the lighting treatments and was therefore selected for further analysis, and its expression rhythm was tightly coupled with core clock components such as CCA1/LHY. BcLhcb1 expression covaried with clock-gene expression, photosynthetic pigment contents, and photosynthetic responses measured under a common reference condition. These associations support a working hypothesis involving a BcLhcb1-associated regulatory module, but do not establish that BcLhcb1 mediates the physiological responses to the lighting treatments. Pn was measured under a common reference condition, and its time integral was interpreted as an index of reference-condition photosynthetic capacity. These findings support further evaluation of alternating lighting schedules, while their effects on actual daily carbon gain and electrical energy efficiency remain to be established. Model simulations identified the 3 h white light + 1 h red-blue combined-light schedule (3L:1X) as the most favorable among the simulated timing schemes, and this regime was subsequently evaluated experimentally. The coordinated responses support an association between clock-gene rhythms, Lhcb1 expression, and photosynthetic acclimation. However, the design does not distinguish the contributions of spectral composition, irradiance, and temporal exposure. The results identify an alternating-light regime for further evaluation using intensity-matched controls. These results suggest that alternating white and red-blue light may provide a promising temporal lighting strategy for modulating circadian and photosynthetic responses in pak choi.

papers.title: PSG diagnostic features of OSAHS in Chinese children: a retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the clinical utility of PSG in diagnosing and characterizing PSG features of OSAHS in children. A retrospective study was implemented from January 2024 to June 2025.A total of 106 children with sleep-related symptoms underwent standardized overnight PSG. Core indicators ‒ Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI), minimum oxygen saturation, sleep efficiency, N3 sleep stage proportion (slow-wave sleep ratio), and arousal index ‒ were analyzed. The OSAHS group had higher AHI, ODI, and arousal index but lower N3 proportion and minimum SpO2 (all p < 0.05). No significant age-group differences were observed (p > 0.05). The mild OSAHS group showed higher sleep efficiency and minimum SpO2, and fewer arousals than moderate/severe groups (p < 0.05). OSAHS detection rate was significantly higher in snoring versus non-snoring children (p < 0.05). Obese children had significantly higher AHI, ODI, and arousal index than non-obese children (p < 0.05). PSG objectively reflects OSAHS severity in children. Children with OSAHS commonly exhibit sleep architecture disruption and hypoxia, which are associated with daytime functional impairments. PSG results guide individualized treatment planning plans.

papers.title: Development and validation of a multimodal data-based scale for predicting epilepsy surgery outcomes.
papers.abstract: Seizure outcomes after drug-resistant epilepsy surgery are hard to predict, and existing models lack rigorous validation. We developed and internally validated a multimodal scale predicting seizure freedom. Retrospectively, 157 of 816 screened patients with complete data and ≥ 1 year follow-up were analyzed (116 seizure-free [SF], 41 non-seizure-free [NSF]). Predictors came from clinical variables, MRI, FDG-PET, video-EEG, and MEG. From 56 variables, eight predictors were fixed by screening, clinical judgment, four machine-learning algorithms, and minimum-AIC logistic regression, then re-estimated in all 157 patients by Firth's bias-corrected logistic regression without repeat selection. Internal validation used 2000 bootstrap resamples. A cutoff maximizing 0.4 ×sensitivity + 0.6 ×specificity was selected once in the full cohort and applied unchanged to the ≥ 24 months subgroup. The model retained disease duration, age at surgery, four EEG patterns, temporal MRI lesion, and unilateral unifocal PET hypometabolism. Development-phase AUCs (0.864 training, 0.810 test) were descriptive. Firth re-estimation gave an apparent AUC of 0.771 and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.724 (Brier 0.156/0.176). At the 79.64-point cutoff, sensitivity was 61.2% and specificity 85.4%; all 95% confidence intervals included the null. Among 101 patients followed ≥ 24 months, the locked model gave AUC 0.770 (95% CI 0.664-0.865), Brier 0.158, sensitivity 53.9%, specificity 96.0%. Multimodal data integration yielded a fully specified, reproducible eight-variable scale with stable discrimination in longer-term follow-up, supporting exploratory use for preoperative risk stratification and counseling alongside presurgical evaluation. Prospective multicenter validation is the next step toward clinical implementation.

papers.title: ST-M2EDA: spatio-temporal metric-guided multi-stream expert domain adaptation network for fatigue monitoring.
papers.abstract: In the human-machine collaboration paradigms of Industry 5.0, the intrinsic non-stationarity and domain drift of electroencephalogram (EEG) signals pose significant challenges to fatigue monitoring. Consequently, achieving accurate and robust cross-subject fatigue detection is paramount for workplace safety. This paper proposes a Spatio-Temporal Metric-Guided Multi-Stream Expert Domain Adaptation Network (ST-M 2 EDA). The framework initially employs Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)-based signal reconstruction to attenuate non-stationary noise, followed by Mixup data augmentation to enhance and smooth the feature space distribution. Furthermore, a hybrid architecture integrating Domain-Specific Batch Normalization (DSBN) with a ResNet-Transformer backbone is constructed to precisely decouple statistical discrepancies between domains. Finally, Multi-Kernel Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MK-MMD) is introduced as a dynamic routing criterion to facilitate fine-grained, adaptive decision-making for target samples. Experimental results on the SEED-VIG dataset demonstrate an average accuracy of 90.54%. Visual analysis of brain topography confirms that the model successfully aligns distributional shifts caused by individual heterogeneity-specifically correcting for specific frontotemporal lobe activation observed in subject S7-and establishes distinct decision boundaries. These findings indicate that synergizing signal reconstruction with Spatio-Temporal metric-guided multi-stream experts effectively mitigates negative transfer, ensuring reliable fatigue detection in complex cross-subject tasks.

papers.title: A phase-calibrated combined electrical-sensory neuromodulation platform for short-Term frontoparietal network modulation and cognitive fatigue resistance.
papers.abstract: Non-invasive multimodal neuromodulation is often limited by cross-modal temporal misalignment caused by modality-specific conduction delays. To address this challenge, we developed a microcontroller-based multiphysics stimulation platform integrating transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) with visual and auditory rhythmic inputs. A feedforward delaycompensation strategy using individualized ERP latencies (visual P1 and auditory N1) was implemented to reduce intermodal timing discrepancies.The system was evaluated in a randomized, sham-controlled crossover study with 15 participants providing complete EEG datasets. Compared with sensory-only stimulation, the phase-coordinated multiphysics condition increased resting-state frontoparietal theta power and enhanced functional connectivity (wPLI). During a subsequent high-load cognitive task, it was also associated with reduced accumulation of fatigue-related parietal alpha power.Exploratory analysis revealed a moderate association between parietal alpha stability and behavioral performance (r = 0.577, p = 0.024). These findings suggest that temporally coordinated cross-modal stimulation may support more stable large-scale neural dynamics and improved cognitive performance under sustained load, providing a technical framework for precision multimodal neuromodulation.

papers.title: Exchange of High-Frequency Medical Monitoring Data Using Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources for Interoperable Integration Into Clinical Practice and Research: Methodological Development Study.
papers.abstract: Continuous patient monitoring generates vast volumes of high-frequency monitoring data, such as electrocardiogram, electroencephalography, and invasive blood pressure tracings, that are often persisted in heterogeneous, noninteroperable formats, limiting integration with electronic health records and secondary use. Although Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) supports general health data exchange, native support for high-frequency medical monitoring data, including associated metadata and data quality metrics, remains limited. This study aims to develop a modality-agnostic FHIR package implementing a Metadata-Proxy pattern to enable scalable, semantically precise representation of high-frequency medical monitoring data, decoupling structured clinical metadata from raw signal storage. This study provides the FHIR package Time Series Integration and Data in Endpoints (TIDE), a collection of FHIR Release 4 artifacts for interoperable exchange and the standardization of high-frequency monitoring clinical data, using electroencephalography as the primary use case while remaining applicable to generic medical monitoring data. The core TIDE Observation profile separates technical metadata and analytical summaries stored directly in FHIR from high-volume raw data referenced via Endpoint resources. Quantitative results are standardized with pattern slicing, including sampling frequency, statistical summaries, and data quality metrics. Semantic interoperability was achieved through a hybrid terminology binding, using Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms, Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes for modalities, and custom CodeSystems for technical metadata, waveform modalities, channel identifiers, and connection types not covered by standard terminologies. All profiles were authored in FHIR Shorthand and compiled with SUSHI to produce a validated Implementation Guide conformant with the FHIR Release 4 core specification. The resulting framework provides a modality-agnostic structure for high-frequency monitoring data, comprising 7 primary FHIR artifacts that define 16 distinct component slices for metadata and signal analysis results. Observation resources reference associated Device and Endpoint instances, encapsulate acquisition parameters, and link to full-time-series repositories. Controlled vocabularies ensure unambiguous exchange, thereby enabling downstream use in research and decision support. The architecture decouples the metadata layer from the storage layer via a standardized Endpoint extension, enabling efficient querying of signals without retrieving large amounts of raw high-frequency monitoring data. TIDE provides a reusable, standards-compliant framework for integrating continuous high-frequency monitoring data into FHIR-based ecosystems. By separating semantically rich, queryable metadata from raw signal storage, TIDE enables longitudinal patient monitoring and automated signal quality-based triage without requiring modification of existing signal storage infrastructure.

papers.title: What Are Recent Insights Into Pontomedullary Circuits Controlling in REM Sleep?
papers.abstract: Recent studies have identified neurochemically defined neuronal groups in the pons and medulla that have a critical role in initiation, maintenance, and manifestations of REM sleep (REM-on neurons). The sublaterodorsal tegmental nucleus (SLD) in rodents (subcoeruleus nucleus in humans) contains a group of glutamatergic neurons that express corticotrophin-releasing hormone‑binding protein (Crhbp + neurons) that initiate REM sleep and elicit REM sleep atonia by projections to inhibitory neurons of the ventromedial medulla projecting to spinal motor neurons. A reciprocal glutamatergic excitatory loop between these SLD Crhbp + neurons and neurons in the dorsomedial medulla expressing nitric oxide synthase 1 (Nos1+ neurons) form a core circuit that initiates and maintains REM sleep. Other neurochemically defined neuronal groups in the dorsomedial medulla trigger rapid eye movements and other phasic phenomena during REM sleep. Both the ventromedial medulla and the dorsomedial medulla contain GABAergic neurons that promote REM sleep by inhibiting REM-off neurons.

papers.title: Germline Genetic Variants and Epilepsy Surgery Response: Individual Participant Pooled Analysis of 272 Patients.
papers.abstract: Genetic testing is increasingly used in presurgical evaluation, but the yield of resection and ablation across germline genetic epilepsies remains uncertain. We conducted a systematic review of MEDLINE (PubMed) and Scopus and added cases from 3 institutional cohorts and the Pediatric Epilepsy Research Consortium (PERC) databases, including individuals with pathogenic/likely pathogenic germline variants besides tuberous sclerosis who underwent resection or laser ablation. Etiologies were grouped into biologically informed categories (GATORopathies, vascular, overgrowth, copy number variants (CNVs), channelopathies, synaptopathies, and other). Primary outcome was seizure freedom (Engel I) at the last follow-up. Group comparisons used Fisher exact and Kruskal-Wallis tests (α = 0.05; Bonferroni when applicable). Prespecified sensitivity analyses stratified by lesional status, excluded GATORopathies, and restricted to literature-only cases. We included 224 literature cases (65 studies), 36 institutional cases, and 12 PERC cases (n = 272). The median follow-up was 24 months (interquartile range 12-48.0). Seizure freedom was achieved in vascular disorders 14/19 (73.6%), GATORopathies 79/120 (65.8%), CNVs 18/31 (58.0%), overgrowth 9/16 (56.6%), channelopathies 13/43 (30.0%), synaptopathies 4/18 (22.2%), and other 11/25 (44.0%) (overall p < 0.001). Among cases with available imaging results, 208/253 (82.2%) had epileptogenic MRI lesions, including 64% of channelopathies and 80% of the synaptopathies. In univariate contrasts (each category vs all others), odds of seizure freedom were higher for vascular disorders (2.64-fold, 95% CI 0.87-9.65) and GATORopathies (2.41-fold, 95% CI 1.44-4.09), and lower for synaptopathies (∼4.2-fold lower, OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.05-0.77) and channelopathies (∼4.5-fold lower, OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.09-0.48). Direction and magnitude were consistent across prespecified sensitivity analyses (lesional only, literature only, exclusion of GATORopathies). Resective surgeries can be effective in germline genetic epilepsies, but outcomes vary by pathway. Disorders with discrete, lesional substrates (GATORopathies, vascular) show the highest likelihood of seizure freedom, whereas channelopathies and synaptopathies, despite the presence of MRI lesions, have substantially lower yields even in lesional cases. Prospective, genotype-aware surgical registries with standardized reporting (EEG, imaging, and pathology) and time-to-event outcomes are needed to refine the selection of surgical candidates and quantify seizure and non-seizure-related outcomes.

papers.title: Patient-Reported Experiences of Long-Term Recovery and Persistent Psychosocial Burden in NMDAR Encephalitis.
papers.abstract: N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) encephalitis is a rare autoimmune disorder with severe neuropsychiatric symptoms. Although neurologic recovery is often favorable, emerging evidence shows high prevalence of long-term sequelae affecting quality of life. Most studies rely on standardized assessments, leaving patient-reported experiences underexplored. We examined long-term psychosocial outcomes using a mixed-methods approach integrating patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), neuropsychological testing, and semistructured interviews informed by qualitative findings from SAPIENCE Level 1. Sixty-five patients with NMDAR encephalitis were recruited across 3 centers (Berlin, Barcelona, and Lyon) at a median of 7.3 years postonset. Remote assessment included semistructured interviews, validated PROMs (sleep quality, fatigue, depression, anxiety, and quality of life), and neuropsychological testing. Multiple regression models were used to identify factors associated with health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Although 76.9% of patients returned to predisease occupations, substantial long-term burden persisted. Memory deficits dominated the postacute phase (68.8%) and remained most commonly reported at follow-up (29.7%). High rates of fatigue (54.4%), sleep disturbances (49.2%), and anxiety (77%) were observed with strong intercorrelations among symptom domains. Sleep disturbances showed the strongest association with reduced quality of life. Initial misdiagnosis occurred in two-thirds of patients. Despite generally positive health care experiences, 54% reported negative social relationship impacts and 46.2% found return to normalcy challenging. NMDAR encephalitis is associated with persistent multidimensional burden despite favorable global recovery. Sleep disturbance emerges as a central and potentially modifiable determinant of HRQoL, while persistent cognitive and psychosocial challenges underscore the need for integrated long-term care. These findings also highlight the importance of patient-reported and qualitative assessments.

papers.title: Association of musculoskeletal symptoms with physical activity, sedentary behavior and sleep: A secondary analysis of the 2016 to 2017 Chilean National Health Survey.
papers.abstract: Musculoskeletal symptoms are a public health concern because of their association with disability and increased economic burden. In other countries, people with these symptoms report lower physical activity levels, less sleep and more sedentary behavior. Evidence in Chile remains limited. To analyze the association between musculoskeletal symptoms and physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep in the Chilean adult population. A secondary analysis of the 2016 to 2017 Chilean National Health Survey (5472 adults), accounting for its complex sampling design. Musculoskeletal symptoms experienced during the previous seven days were assessed using the Community-Oriented Programme for the Control of Rheumatic Disease Core Questionnaire. Physical activity and sedentary behavior were assessed using the Global Physical Activity Questionnaire, while sleep duration was measured as the self-reported average number of hours per day. Differences in minutes per day were estimated with linear regression, while adherence to recommendations (World Health Organization physical activity guidelines, sedentary time of less than four hours per day, and sleep duration of seven to nine hours per day) was assessed using univariable and adjusted logistic regression models. Musculoskeletal symptoms were present in 38% (95% confidence interval 35 to 41) of adults. Compared to adults without symptoms, those with symptoms had mean differences of 16 minutes per day (95% confidence interval -8 to 40) in total physical activity, 16 minutes per day (95% confidence interval -1 to 33) in sedentary behavior, -16 minutes per day (95% confidence interval -25 to -7) in sleep, 28 minutes per day (95% confidence interval 8 to 49) in work physical activity and -12 minutes per day (95% confidence interval -22 to -3) in travel physical activity. Among adults with symptoms, 36%, 35%, and 48% did not meet the physical activity, sedentary, and sleep recommendations, respectively. No statistically significant associations were found between musculoskeletal symptoms and adherence to any of these recommendations. Adults with musculoskeletal symptoms reported similar levels of total physical activity and sedentary behavior, about 16 fewer minutes of sleep per day, and more work-related physical activity than adults without symptoms. Failure to meet the recommendations was frequent in both groups. Given the cross-sectional study design, prospective studies are needed to clarify the direction of these associations.

papers.title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates single-neuron activity in humans.
papers.abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is an established treatment for depression, yet the fundamental question of how cortical stimulation influences single neurons in deep brain circuits critical for mood regulation remains unanswered. Using a rare opportunity to record from intracranial microelectrodes while TMS was delivered in four neurosurgical patients, we evaluated the responses of 185 single neurons. Artifact cleaning enabled single-neuron spikes to be resolved as early as 8 ms after stimulation. We found that single-pulse TMS to the left dlPFC elicited time-locked firing responses in 46% of neurons (26% facilitated only, 19% suppressed only, 1% both). These responses occurred within deep bilateral cortical and subcortical structures, including the putamen and thalamus. Single-pulse TMS tended to facilitate spiking in striato-thalamic putative inhibitory neurons from ~8 ms, peaking at ~80 to 100 ms, and decaying until ~600 ms. In contrast, putative excitatory neurons and limbic areas were suppressed with a slower time course lasting to ~1,000 ms. TMS-evoked potentials recorded from intracranial depth macroelectrodes to quantify network activity revealed that the modulation of responsive neurons was positively correlated with cortico-striato-thalamic network activity and anticorrelated with limbic network activity in one participant with sufficient network and unit sampling. These results suggest that dlPFC TMS recruits a high percentage of neurons spanning cortical and subcortical brain regions bilaterally. The recruitment pattern selectively involves increasing the firing rate of inhibitory neurons in executive control networks while suppressing limbic excitatory drive, providing a candidate cellular mechanism for how cortical stimulation modulates distributed brain networks.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

papers.title: Occupational Conditions and Sleep Duration, Continuity, and Quality among First Responders: Evidence from the 2025 Los Angeles Wildfires.
papers.abstract: To examine occupational conditions and sleep during wildfire response. We surveyed 90 first responders during the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires and modeled sleep duration, continuity, and quality against shift characteristics, workload, hazard proximity, and working conditions. After adjustment for age and experience, 24-hour shifts were associated with 1.65 fewer total sleep hours (95% CI: -2.45, -0.84) and 1.93 fewer consecutive hours (-2.99, -0.87). Four or more consecutive shifts were also associated with shorter sleep, and poorer working conditions with shorter total sleep; hazard proximity and total shifts were not. Poor or very poor sleep quality (83%) was associated with all exposures except total shifts and shift extension. Long and consecutive shifts were associated with shorter, more fragmented sleep. Exposures were closely tied to occupational role.
papers.journal: Journal of occupational and environmental medicine

papers.title: Music-Based Interventions for People Living With Dementia.
papers.abstract: Dementia is characterized by progressive cognitive decline and behavioral symptoms that significantly impair quality of life for both people living with dementia and their paid and unpaid caregivers. Music-based interventions offer unique therapeutic benefits because musical memory often remains intact in dementia, enabling emotional connection and reminiscence. This article provides a practical framework for home care nurses to implement music interventions across all stages of dementia (early, middle, and late) in the home setting. The evidence suggests that music can reduce agitation, anxiety, depression, and sleep disturbances while promoting social engagement and enhancing mood. Strategies include assessing musical preferences, creating personalized playlists, and integrating music into daily care activities such as bathing or dressing. Nurses should monitor responses and collaborate with family caregivers, while considering the ethical implications of providing music. By tailoring music interventions to individual needs and behavioral symptoms, nurses can improve quality of life for people living with dementia and potentially alleviate family caregiver burden. Current research is synthesized to provide actionable strategies for nursing practice, emphasizing the role of culturally meaningful music and individualized delivery methods.

papers.title: Risk of Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Open-Angle Glaucoma: A Population-Based Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: In this retrospective population-based cohort study, patients with open-angle glaucoma were more likely to develop obstructive sleep apnea than matched controls from the general population of Olmsted County, Minnesota. To investigate the risk of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in patients with open-angle glaucoma (OAG) compared to the risk of OSA in matched controls from a general population. Retrospective population-based case-control study comparing the incidence of OSA with a diagnosis of OAG (cases) to the incidence of OSA in matched patients without OAG (controls) from Olmsted County, Minnesota between January 1, 1980 and December 31, 2018. Patients were identified using the Rochester Epidemiology Project. Medical records were reviewed to confirm OAG diagnoses. OSA diagnoses were based on sleep study data and polysomnography parameters. Cumulative probability of OSA was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. This cohort had 7,000 patients: 3,500 case patients with OAG diagnosed at any time point, and 3,500 matched control subjects without OAG, with all OAG and OSA diagnoses manually confirmed. There was no statistically significant difference of OSA frequency prior to index date in cases versus controls (P=0.52). There were 371 (12.5%) cases who developed OSA after glaucoma diagnosis compared to 297 (10.2%) patients who were diagnosed with OSA after the index date (P=0.0068). The multivariate hazard ratio for diagnosis of OSA after OAG diagnosis was 1.17 (P=0.047, 95% CI: 1.00, 1.36). The 10-year absolute risk of OSA after OAG diagnosis was 12.5%, and risk of OSA increased with time. In this population-based study, patients with OAG were more likely to be diagnosed with OSA compared to patients without OAG, suggesting a possible association that may justify increased clinical awareness.

papers.title: A substituted cysteine accessibility protocol to probe orthosteric and non-canonical ligand binding to ion channels.
papers.abstract: The Substituted Cysteine Accessibility Method (SCAM) is an approach for probing the biophysics and pharmacology of ion channels by targeting covalent modifications to individual amino acids. Here, we present a protocol to constrain channel stoichiometry and identify asymmetric or non-canonical ligand-binding sites using SCAM followed by electrophysiology in mammalian heterologous expression systems, in the context of heteropentameric nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. This protocol is applicable to examination of multiple channel properties, including ligand binding, gating, pore conductance, and selectivity. For complete information on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Kulkarni et al.1.

papers.title: What exercise regimen is most effective for improving sleep quality in older adults? a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Exercise benefits sleep quality in older adults, yet the effects of different exercise intervention types across various parameters (duration, intensity, frequency, and period) remain unclear. This network meta-analysis aimed to compare the effects of different intervention types across these parameters on sleep quality in older adults, providing an evidence-based basis for formulating scientific exercise prescriptions. Relevant randomized controlled trials were retrieved from five databases (including Web of Science) up to November 15, 2025. Two researchers independently extracted data. Study quality was assessed using RevMan, and network meta-analysis was conducted via Stata. Publication bias was examined with funnel plots and Egger's test, intervention effects were ranked by SUCRA, and leave-one-out sensitivity analysis was used to verify result robustness. A total of 32 randomized controlled trials involving 2,658 participants were included. Network meta-analysis showed that combined exercise (SUCRA=74.8%) may have ranked first, followed by aerobic exercise (65.4%), resistance exercise (64.4%), mind-body exercise (49.7%), and dance (46.1%). Subgroup analyses indicated that the rankings of exercise types might vary according to single-session duration, weekly frequency, intervention period, exercise intensity, and participant characteristics. Combined exercise may demonstrate the optimal effect on sleep quality improvement in older adults, followed by aerobic exercise and resistance exercise. The intervention efficacy of each exercise type may vary with intervention parameters and participant characteristics rather than remaining fixed. However, these findings should be regarded as provisional. Given the limited number of included studies, these preliminary conclusions require further validation through high-quality research.

papers.title: The relevance of sleep and chronopsychology in understanding maladaptive behaviors in eating disorders: A narrative review.
papers.abstract: Circadian disruption and sleep-wake dysregulation have been increasingly linked to psychiatric conditions, yet their role in eating disorders and addiction-like maladaptive behaviors remains insufficiently examined in an integrative framework. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on chronotype, circadian misalignment, sleep features, and behavioral addictions across anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, orthorexic tendencies, and night eating syndrome. Literature published between 1970 and 2025 was identified through PubMed, Google Scholar, and reference screening, focusing on chronobiological, sleep-related, neuroendocrine, and behavioral aspects of eating disorders. Delayed sleep timing, eveningness preference, and insomnia symptoms commonly co-occur with disordered eating. Findings suggest overlapping mechanisms linking circadian dysregulation, sleep-related and compulsive, reward-driven behaviors, including binge eating and compensatory practices. Objective measures indicate alterations in sleep continuity, slow-wave sleep, and REM parameters. Neuroendocrine evidence further supports links among biological rhythms, appetite regulation, and sleep regulation. Preliminary chronotherapeutic interventions, such as light exposure and sleep phase modification, show promise but remain insufficiently tested. Overall, subclinical, clinical and emerging eating disorders remain underrepresented in chronobiological research. Circadian misalignment may represent a clinically relevant and modifiable dimension underlying maladaptive eating behaviors. However, fragmented evidence and methodological limitations restrict firm conclusions. A structured research agenda is proposed to guide future integrative research.

papers.title: Respiratory self-similarity is a sleep apnea endotype that predicts cardiovascular disease related mortality.
papers.abstract: Pathological respiratory chemoreflex activation (high loop gain) in sleep apnea may activate the carotid body and induce excessive sympathetic nerve output, and independently add to the risk of adverse outcomes. This study aims to determine whether a high loop gain of the respiratory control system during sleep, estimated by respiratory self-similarity (SS) and the algorithm-derived central respiratory event index (CREI), is associated with new-onset cardiovascular disease (CVD) and CVD-related mortality. A secondary analysis of The Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS) and Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). High SS% and CREI were defined as the highest quartile. Lasso regression and restricted cubic spline assessed the relationship between SS%, CREI and CVD, CVD-mortality and all-cause mortality. A cumulative incidence function and a Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard model were used to evaluate this outcome accounting for competing risks. In adjusted models with age as a categorical variable divided by 65 years old, the highest quartile of SS% (HR 1.693, p: 0.017 in MESA and HR 1.240, p : 0.009 in SHHS) was associated with the incidence of CVD and was more prominent in males. A positive relationship between SS% (MESA: HR 1.429, p: 0.039; SHHS HR1.176, p:0.018 ) for the continuous metrics and CVD mortality in both cohorts was more apparent in men than in women. The categorical high-exposure association with CVD mortality was not consistent across cohorts.The associations were significantly attenuated when adjusted by age as a continuous metric. An endotype of sleep apnea reflecting high loop gain is associated with CVD and CVD mortality, especially in males.

papers.title: Atypical Atrial Flutter From Lipomatous Hypertrophy of the Interatrial Septum in a Procedure-Naive Patient.
papers.abstract: Lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum (LHIS) is generally benign and often discovered incidentally; however, it can occasionally serve as a substrate for atrial arrhythmias. An 86-year-old man with no prior cardiac history presented with new onset atrial flutter (AFL) with an atrial rate of 280 beats/min. During an electrophysiology study, intracardiac echocardiography identified LHIS. Three-dimensional electroanatomic activation mapping demonstrated the earliest focal activation at the superior posteroseptal right atrium, corresponding to the location of the LHIS. Radiofrequency ablation at this site terminated the AFL, rendering the tachycardia noninducible. LHIS can act as an isolated arrhythmogenic substrate for atypical AFL. The combination of intracardiac echocardiography and high-density electroanatomic mapping allows precise localization of the arrhythmogenic focus, facilitating safe and effective catheter ablation. LHIS should be considered a potential arrhythmogenic substrate in patients with atypical AFL. Catheter ablation of LHIS-associated AFL is safe and effective.

papers.title: Gotta Go Fast: Intended Concentric Effort Produces Divergent Myoelectric Spectral Profiles During Fatiguing, Load-Equated Resistance Exercise.
papers.abstract: Benitez, B, Kwak, M, Succi, PJ, Mitchinson, CJ, Snell, ER, and Bergstrom, HC. Gotta go fast: Intended concentric effort produces divergent myoelectric spectral profiles during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine how intended concentric velocity, that is, the volitional effort applied to accelerate a load, influences the spectral characteristics of the surface electromyographic (sEMG) signal during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. Twenty recreationally active adults (10 men and 10 women) performed unilateral leg extensions to task failure at 70% 1 repetition maximum under 2 within-participant conditions as follows: maximal intended concentric velocity (Vmax) and 50% of individualized Vmax (50%Vmax). Bipolar sEMG from the vastus lateralis was decomposed into 10 frequency bands using wavelet-based time-frequency analysis. Band-specific spectral intensities were modeled with a lognormal generalized linear mixed-effects model, and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (ρc) was computed between condition-specific spectral profiles across pairwise time points. The mean propulsive concentric velocity and total repetitions to task failure were secondary outcomes. Significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. The 3-way interaction of condition × frequency × repetition was significant (χ2(3) = 23.98, p < 0.001). Across the set, Vmax redistributed spectral power bidirectionally, increasing the low bands while suppressing the high bands, whereas 50%Vmax increased across the entire spectrum without high-frequency suppression. Despite these divergent profiles, the conditions converged at task failure (ρc = 0.98), and the convergence was asymmetric. The fatigued 50%Vmax profile approximated the fresh Vmax profile (ρc = 0.97) rather than the reverse (ρc = 0.74), indicating that submaximal effort approached the maximal-effort state as fatigue accumulated. The mean propulsive concentric velocity also declined 3.6 times more steeply under Vmax despite similar repetitions. Intended concentric velocity appears to shape the spectral profile of muscle excitation under fixed loading.
papers.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research

papers.title: Diagnostic value of extending outpatient EEG to record sleep - A retrospective study.
papers.abstract: Evidence for the utility of sleep electroencephalography (EEG) in the diagnosis of epilepsy is inconsistent, often necessitating repeat visits and sleep deprivation (SD), which increases patient and resource burden. In our setting in India, patients are often referred for EEG immediately following consultation (single visit) and EEG sessions are extended to allow for spontaneous sleep acquisition without prior SD. We aimed to evaluate the success rate of achieving sleep during these extended outpatient recordings and its incremental diagnostic yield for interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs). We retrospectively analyzed 1762 outpatient EEGs from patients (45% female) with suspected or known epilepsy. All patients underwent an extended routine EEG (~40-50 min), incorporating standard activation procedures and aiming to capture spontaneous sleep where possible. Successful sleep acquisition was defined as the attainment of at least NREM stage N2. IED detection rates were compared between wakefulness and sleep across different epilepsy types. Sleep was achieved in 70.5% of patients (median age, 28 years; IQR: 16-55; range, 0.3-90). The proportion attaining sleep increased with recording duration, from 36.7% at 20 min to 55.6% at 30 min and 66.7% at 50 min, with a median time to sleep onset of 20 min. Among 1199 patients with both awake and sleep states captured, wakefulness identified IEDs in 29% (n = 350), while sleep captured unique IEDs in an additional 12% (n = 141), increasing the total yield significantly. In a sub-analysis of confirmed epilepsy cases (n = 751), wakefulness showed IEDs in 42% (n = 315), with sleep adding another 16% (n = 123). The diagnostic yield of sleep recordings was significantly higher than that of wakefulness alone (OR: 1.31; 95% CI: 1.02-1.68; p = 0.043), particularly among adults with idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE) (OR: 2.20; 95% CI: 1.30-3.73; p = 0.004) and children with self-limited epilepsy (OR: ∞; p = 0.031). Despite a busy outpatient setting, 70.5% of patients attained N2 sleep during an extended EEG recording without SD. Sleep capture increased progressively with recording duration, with the greatest incremental gain between 20 and 30 min, suggesting that a modest extension beyond 20 min substantially increases the likelihood of capturing sleep. Sleep recording increased IED detection over wakefulness alone, particularly in children, in adults with IGE, and in self-limited epilepsies. Whether this approach can substitute for a sleep-deprived EEG requires prospective, head-to-head evaluation.
