papers.title: Response to "From spectral parameterization to spectral staging in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder".
The neuropathic chameleon: we are hot on the scent.
papers.abstract: A common chronic pain condition, neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory or neural tissue and is characterized by a combination of negative (eg, numbness) and positive (eg, burning pain) sensory symptoms that significantly affect the quality of life. Common comorbidities such as depression and sleep disruption contribute to a substantial disease burden, which is further exacerbated by the apparent lack of effective therapeutic options. Current treatment options frequently achieve only partial, insufficient pain relief or may be completely ineffective in a considerable number of patients. The development of new drugs has thus far achieved moderate success, with many clinical trials failing to meet their primary endpoints; thus, a substantial unmet clinical need persists. One reason for this therapeutic deadlock is the considerable heterogeneity of neuropathic pain, driven by diverse pathophysiological mechanisms that vary between patients regardless of the underlying disease etiology. Accordingly, reclassification efforts follow a mechanism-based approach that reflects pathophysiological pain generators rather than disease etiology. Although diagnosis remains anchored in lesion- or disease-based criteria and structured clinical assessment, treatment development increasingly benefits from mechanism-informed phenotyping. A priori stratification based on individual mechanisms may help identify treatment responders, but implementation requires surrogate markers, as no biomarkers for pain mechanisms currently exist. In this article, we discuss candidate predictive markers and surrogate markers, focusing on sensory symptoms and signs assessed through patient-reported outcome measures and sensory testing, and their integration into future clinical trials.

papers.title: An integrative view of human nociceptor diversity: from microneurography to molecular identity.
papers.abstract: Neuropathic pain arises from dysfunction of the peripheral or central nervous system and affects up to 10% of the population worldwide. Aberrant activity in injured sensory nerve fibers, particularly spontaneous firing and altered conduction properties of nociceptors, is tightly linked to pain, yet its molecular underpinnings in humans have long remained elusive. Over recent years, major technological advances have transformed both functional and molecular analyses of sensory neurons. High-resolution single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have produced detailed atlases of sensory neuron diversity, while traditional electrophysiological approaches such as patch-clamp and microneurography have provided unparalleled insight into nerve fiber properties. Despite their individual strengths, molecular and functional classifications of sensory neurons have largely evolved in parallel. This review focuses on emerging strategies that bridge these approaches to achieve an integrated, mechanistic understanding of neuropathic pain. We discuss how microneurography-defined biophysical hallmarks, such as activity-dependent slowing, recovery cycle signatures, and following frequency, can be transferred into in vitro patch-clamp paradigms, enabling direct functional comparison with dissociated human and large-animal sensory neurons. The incorporation of Patch-seq approaches has further enabled the assignment of molecular identity to functionally defined nociceptor subtypes, exemplified by the characterization of the mechano-insensitive "sleeping" nociceptors. Finally, we highlight how multimodal datasets combining electrophysiology, transcriptomics, and computational modeling provide new opportunities to unravel the ion channel mechanisms, particularly sodium channel subtypes, that shape pathological firing states. By directly linking human nerve fiber function to molecular programs, this integrative framework paves the way toward stratified, mechanism-based therapies for neuropathic pain.

papers.title: The pharmacological frontier in obstructive sleep apnoea: From pathophysiologic endotypes to precision medicine.
papers.abstract: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea (OSA) is a prevalent global health crisis with limited real-world effectiveness of Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) due to suboptimal adherence. Modern understanding has shifted from a purely mechanical model to the PALM Scale, which identifies anatomical and non-anatomical endotypes: Pcrit (Anatomy), Arousal threshold, Loop gain and Muscle responsiveness. This review synthesises current pharmacological advances targeting these specific endotypes to provide alternatives for CPAP-intolerant patients. We analysed landmark clinical trials including SURMOUNT-OSA (Tirzepatide), SCALE (Liraglutide), FLOW TRIAL (Sulthiame) and MARIPOSA (AD109). This review showed Incretin-based therapies (e.g., Tirzepatide) produce large and clinically meaningful reductions in Apnoea-Hypopnea Index (AHI), often exceeding 40-50% in many patients. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., Sulthiame) stabilise ventilatory instability (Loop Gain), reducing AHI by approximately 40%. Combined noradrenergic-antimuscarinic agents (e.g., AD109) enhance upper airway muscle responsiveness. Furthermore, Solriamfetol and Pitolisant effectively manage residual daytime sleepiness in PAP-adherent patients. So the management of OSA is entering an era of Precision Medicine. Pharmacotherapy may serve as an adjunct to PAP, and in selected phenotypes, could function as a potential alternative option, particularly in the Indian 'thin-fat' phenotype (normal BMI with central adiposity and visceral fat), where CPAP adherence remains challenging.
papers.journal: Lung India : official organ of Indian Chest Society

papers.title: Ultrasonographic assessment of diaphragmatic functions in relation to obstructive sleep apnea severity.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) affects 9-38% of adults and is associated with intermittent hypoxia, sleep fragmentation, and increased cardiovascular risk. Although the diaphragm contributes 60-80% of ventilatory effort, diaphragmatic functional changes in OSA remain inadequately characterized. Diaphragmatic ultrasonography offers a noninvasive, bedside method for functional assessment, but evidence in OSA is limited. To evaluate diaphragmatic function using ultrasonography in patients evaluated for suspected OSA and to determine its association with disease severity. This prospective cross-sectional study included 62 patients evaluated for suspected OSA attending inpatient and outpatient services at a tertiary care center between January 2024 and April 2025. OSA severity was classified using polysomnography-derived Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) as per American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) guidelines. Blinded ultrasonographic assessment measured right and left hemidiaphragm thickness, thickening fraction, and diaphragmatic excursion. Statistical analysis included Spearman's correlation, Kruskal-Wallis test, ordinal logistic regression, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. The mean age was 51 years, with male predominance (72.6%). Most participants were overweight or obese. The median AHI was 25.6 events/hour, and severe OSA was present in 41.9% of participants, while mild OSA constituted 37.1%, reflecting referral-based nature of the cohort. None of the enrolled patients had AHI < 5. Left diaphragmatic excursion showed a weak positive correlation with AHI (ρ = 0.274; P = 0.031) and a multivariable-adjusted association with OSA severity (OR 1.125; 95% CI 1.026-1.249; P = 0.017). For identifying moderate-to-severe OSA, diaphragmatic ultrasonography demonstrated an AUC of 0.72 (95% CI 0.59-0.85; P = 0.002), with 66.1% accuracy, 59.0% sensitivity, and 78.3% specificity. Diaphragmatic function assessed by ultrasonography is largely preserved in OSA, with left diaphragmatic excursion showing a multivariable-adjusted association with disease severity, these findings primarily reflect a mixed-severity population with a substantial proportion of mild OSA. Bedside diaphragmatic ultrasound may serve as an exploratory adjunct for OSA risk stratification, particularly in resource-limited settings, pending external validation.
papers.journal: Lung India : official organ of Indian Chest Society

papers.title: Diaphragm Weakness and Sleep-Related Breathing Disorders in Patients with Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathy.
papers.abstract: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIMs) can cause respiratory muscle weakness, leading to diaphragm weakness (DW) and sleep-related breathing disorders (SRBD). We aimed to investigate clinical findings of DW and SRBD in patients with IIMs. In patients with biopsy-confirmed IIMs, demographics, respiratory symptoms, single-breath counting (SBC), arterial blood gas, upright/supine SpO2 and spirometry, diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO), maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressure (MIP, MEP), peak cough flow (PCF), and polysomnography parameters were prospectively evaluated. Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), STOP-BANG, and Mallampati scores were recorded. The presence of at least one of two findings was considered suggestive of DW: (1) paradoxical abdominal movement (PAM), (2) upright-supine forced vital capacity (FVC) difference of ≥20%. Sixteen patients (12 female/4 male, mean age: 54.4 ± 11.2/y, 9 dermatomyositis [DM], 6 polymyositis [PM], 1 inclusion body myositis [IBM]) were evaluated. Findings consistent with DW were observed in 25% of patients, and all of them had DM. MIP, MEP, and PCF were reduced in the majority of patients. Supine FVC% and supine SpO2 were significantly lower in patients with DW (P = .001 and P = .003, respectively). PaO2, SaO2, SBC, and PCF were lower, and the upright-supine SpO₂ difference was greater in patients with DW, although these differences were not statistically significant. Polysomnography was performed in 68.8% (n = 11) of patients. All 11 patients who underwent polysomnography had obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) (2 severe, 4 moderate, 5 mild). Findings suggestive of DW were observed in 25% of patients with IIM and exclusively in those with DM, while OSA was identified in all patients who underwent polysomnography. These findings may support the clinical evaluation of both diaphragm involvement and sleep-related breathing disorders in patients with IIM.

papers.title: Effect of Aromatherapy on Sleep Quality among Hospitalized Patients.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbance is a frequent concern among hospitalized patients and is influenced by illness, anxiety, environmental noise, lighting, and routine medical care. Poor sleep during hospitalization can negatively affect immune function, wound healing, and recovery outcomes. Although pharmacological sleep aids are commonly used, they are often associated with adverse effects such as dependency, confusion, and increased risk of falls. Consequently, interest has increased in nonpharmacological interventions such as aromatherapy. Nonpharmacological interventions such as aromatherapy may offer a safe and effective alternative. To assess sleep quality among hospitalized patients, evaluate the effect of aromatherapy on sleep quality, and determine the association between sleep quality and selected demographic variables. A quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design was conducted among 60 adult patients admitted to selected hospitals in Pimpri, Pune. Participants were selected using purposive sampling and allocated to experimental (n = 30) and control (n = 30) groups. The experimental group received lavender essential oil aromatherapy through diffusion for three consecutive nights, while the control group received routine care. Sleep quality was assessed using a standardized sleep quality assessment tool. Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics. The experimental group showed a statistically significant improvement in sleep quality following aromatherapy, with mean scores increasing from 1.9 in the pretest to 3.0 in the posttest (t = 7.50, P < 0.05). No significant improvement was observed in the control group. No significant association was found between sleep quality and selected demographic variables. Aromatherapy using lavender essential oil is an effective, safe, and noninvasive intervention for improving sleep quality among hospitalized patients.

papers.title: Perimenopause and cardiometabolic risk: emerging evidence, therapeutic opportunities and unanswered questions.
papers.abstract: Perimenopause is increasingly recognized as a critical period for cardiometabolic health. During the years surrounding the final menstrual period, adverse changes in lipid profiles, insulin sensitivity, body composition and vascular function accelerate beyond those expected from aging alone, concurrent with the emergence and peak severity of menopause symptoms. Accumulating evidence suggests that vasomotor symptoms and sleep disturbance are associated with adverse cardiometabolic profiles and increased cardiovascular disease risk. Mechanistic data indicate that autonomic dysregulation, inflammation and neuroendocrine systems may represent shared pathways linking symptom burden and cardiometabolic dysfunction. Complementing these findings, prospective studies demonstrate that poor cardiovascular health and metabolic dysfunction may predict subsequent symptom development, suggesting that cardiometabolic health influences the menopause transition experience itself. Together, these findings support a model in which perimenopause represents a physiologic convergence point where symptom burden and cardiometabolic risk intersect, with implications for symptom management and primary prevention. However, major evidence gaps remain, including the absence of interventional studies during perimenopause and uncertainty regarding whether these relationships are causal or therapeutically modifiable. Future research should determine whether targeting cardiometabolic health during this window can improve both cardiovascular outcomes and the symptom experience of the menopause transition.
papers.journal: Climacteric : the journal of the International Menopause Society

papers.title: Preoperative Oral Esketamine for Perioperative Comfort in Children Undergoing Adenotonsillectomy: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Dose-Finding Study.
papers.abstract: Pediatric adenotonsillectomy often causes preoperative anxiety, venous cannulation pain, and emergence agitation. Esketamine has multimodal properties, but the optimal oral dose for children is unknown. This study evaluated oral esketamine at 1, 2, and 3 mg/kg for perioperative comfort. In this randomized double-blind trial, 99 children (ASA I-II, 1-6 years) received oral 10% glucose (control, n = 26) or esketamine 1 mg/kg (EK1, n = 26), 2 mg/kg (EK2, n = 23), or 3 mg/kg (EK3, n = 24) 30 min before anesthesia. Ramsay Sedation Scale (RSS) and FLACC pain score at venous cannulation, and PAED score at 15 min after extubation. remifentanil use, postoperative FLACC (2-48 h), sleep quality, and adverse events. All esketamine doses improved sedation and analgesia at cannulation (overall p < 0.001), with largest effect at 3 mg/kg. Median RSS (IQR): control 1.00 (1.00-2.00); EK1 2.00 (1.75-3.00, p = 0.028); EK2 2.00 (1.00-3.00, p = 0.049); EK3 3.00 (2.00-3.37, p < 0.001). FLACC scores: control 6.00 (3.00-7.00); EK1 2.50 (1.00-4.00, p = 0.016); EK2 2.00 (0.00-4.00, p = 0.001); EK3 0.00 (0.00-1.75, p < 0.001). PAED score at 15 min was lower in EK2 than control (5.00 [2.00-10.00] vs. 10.00 [6.00-12.00], p = 0.048). Remifentanil consumption was reduced in EK3 (120.00 [80.00-159.50] vs. 240.00 [160.00-315.00] μg, p = 0.001). Postoperative pain at 2-6 h was lower in EK2 and EK3 (p < 0.05), persisting to 48 h in EK3 (p < 0.05). Sleep quality improved in EK3 at 24 h (p = 0.023) and 48 h (p = 0.032). Adverse events did not differ significantly. Preoperative oral esketamine (1-3 mg/kg) enhances perioperative comfort in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy. The 2 mg/kg dose offers the best balance of efficacy and safety, while 3 mg/kg provides superior analgesia and opioid sparing.

papers.title: Coverage Criteria vs. Clinical Reality: Navigating Medicaid Barriers to Tirzepatide Access.
papers.abstract: Medicaid beneficiaries often face barriers to accessing evidence-based metabolic therapies, even as U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) indications for agents such as tirzepatide expand. Although tirzepatide is approved for type 2 diabetes (T2D), obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and obesity, some state Medicaid programs apply diagnosis-based restrictions that do not align with FDA labeling or clinical practice. We describe a 34-year-old woman with obesity, T2D, and OSA who experienced repeated denials for tirzepatide under Ohio Medicaid, despite meeting FDA-approved criteria for multiple indications. Diagnostic silos, contradictory exclusion rules, and inconsistent authorization pathways delayed treatment for six months, requiring multiple appeals, peer-to-peer reviews, and a state hearing before approval. This case illustrates how rigid coverage criteria can override clinical judgment and impede timely treatment. Variation across Medicaid programs limits access to glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-based therapies. Aligning coverage with FDA labeling is essential to ensuring equitable, patient-centered care for underserved populations.
papers.journal: Journal of health care for the poor and underserved

papers.title: Sleep and Cardiometabolic Disease: A Wearable-Electronic Health Record Study in the US All of Us Research Program.
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep health spans duration, quality, regularity, and timing, yet Life's Essential 8 scores sleep by duration alone, and regularity studies used about 1 week of data. How these dimensions, measured over months, relate to incident cardiometabolic disease is unknown, as is whether nightly sleep-cycle structure adds information. Methods: This cohort study included US adults in the All of Us Research Program with linked Fitbit and electronic health records (2009-2023). We derived 11 sleep metrics over a 180-day baseline (≥90 valid nights). Incident diagnoses, grouped into phecodes, were counted after a 180-day washout to limit reverse causation. Primary analyses related these metrics to prespecified endpoints, including a CVD composite (myocardial infarction, heart failure, cardiomyopathy, or ischemic stroke), heart failure, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. Cox models adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle, and comorbidity factors. Exploratory analyses examined wearable-estimated sleep cycles (7,199 participants; 1,017,812 sleep-stage nights). Results: Among 10,362 participants (median age, 53 years; 70% female), 230 developed the CVD composite (median follow-up, 3.7 years). Each 1-SD (29-minute) higher night-to-night variability in sleep duration was associated with higher CVD composite risk (hazard ratio, 1.24 [95% CI, 1.09-1.41]), as was higher variability in bedtime (1.23 [1.10-1.37]), waketime (1.20 [1.09-1.32]), and midpoint (1.21 [1.09-1.35]); mean sleep duration was not (0.96 [0.85-1.08]). Variability in sleep duration was also associated with heart failure (1.32 [1.13-1.55]), hypertension (1.16 [1.08-1.25]), and type 2 diabetes (1.20 [1.07-1.35]). More sleep cycles were associated with lower atrial arrhythmia risk (0.72 [0.58-0.89]), independent of sleep duration, regularity, and timing (0.58 [0.44-0.77]). Conclusions: Night-to-night irregularity in sleep duration and timing was associated with the CVD composite, heart failure, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes; mean duration was not associated with the CVD composite. More wearable-estimated sleep cycles were associated with lower atrial arrhythmia risk beyond conventional sleep metrics, a novel finding requiring confirmation.

papers.title: Restitution properties during ventricular fibrillation and the effects of cardiac pacing location on ventricular electrophysiology in the rabbit heart.
papers.abstract: Sudden cardiac death is a cause of mortality due to malignant arrhythmias such as ventricular fibrillation (VF). Although action potential duration (APD) restitution is a method to assess arrhythmic susceptibility, repolarisation may depend on prior activation history, a phenomenon known as cardiac memory. Cardiac memory describes the persistence of repolarisation effects from previous beats, such that APD reflects not only the immediately preceding diastolic interval (DI) but also earlier activation effects. This may be relevant during VF, where continuously varying activation patterns prevent a steady electrophysiological state. This study investigated how pacing location affects ventricular electrophysiology and whether repolarisation during VF exhibits short-term cardiac memory. Langendorff-perfused rabbit hearts were used to record monophasic action potentials from the left ventricular apex and base. Pacing was conducted from five sites. Steady-state APD was assessed during constant pacing. Effective refractory period (ERP), APD restitution and conduction time restitution (CTR) were assessed using an S1-S2 extra-stimulus protocol (S1, conditioning stimuli; S2, premature extra-stimulus). Additionally, APD-DI and APD-APD relationships were analysed during early VF. Pacing location significantly influenced S1 and S2 conduction delays, consistent with site-dependent activation timing. However, steady-state APD, ERP and CTR were not significantly affected by pacing location. In contrast, during VF, APD exhibited a significant dependence on preceding DI and preceding APD over approximately the first 30 beats, with these relationships progressively deteriorating thereafter. These findings demonstrate that while pacing location alters activation timing, repolarisation dynamics under stable activation histories are robust. During VF, continuously changing activation patterns unmask short-term cardiac memory.

papers.title: CircaVal: a gene-centric multi-omics platform for exploring circadian regulatory features.
papers.abstract: The circadian clock orchestrates daily physiological processes through coordinated regulation of clock-controlled gene expression across multiple molecular layers. However, systematic characterization of this multilayered rhythmic regulation remains challenging because relevant information is distributed across independent datasets and rhythmicity is evaluated using diverse analytical approaches. Here, we developed CircaVal, a gene-centric multi-omics platform for the integrated exploration and interpretation of circadian regulatory features in humans, mice, and baboons. To support this framework, CircaVal processes public datasets using standardized, data-type-specific pipelines, and gene rhythmicity is integrated with tissue-specific expression, cross-species orthology, functional annotations, and multi-omics regulatory features. CircaVal further introduces an integrated rhythmicity score (IRS), which combines concordance across multiple rhythm-detection methods with reproducibility across independent datasets to provide a quantitative basis for prioritizing candidate rhythmic genes. The platform enables users to examine gene rhythmicity across datasets, identify tissue-enriched rhythmic genes, compare rhythmicity across species, and explore associated regulatory features. Additional functions include interactive gene-centric exploration, genome-browser visualization, rhythmicity analysis of user-uploaded time-series data, and programmatic data access. Together, these capabilities provide an integrated framework for rhythmic gene prioritization and gene-level interpretation of circadian regulatory features across tissues, species, datasets, and omics data types. CircaVal is freely available at https://CircaVal.com.

papers.title: Effects of far-infrared radiation on the nervous system and their potential.
papers.abstract: Far-infrared radiation (FIR; 3-1000 μm) is characterized by its strong tissue penetration and efficient heat conduction properties. Specifically, wavelengths within the range of 8-14 μm-often referred to as growth rays-are efficiently absorbed by living organisms, generating pronounced thermal effects. These wavelengths closely correspond to the natural vibrational wavelength of water molecules, thus enabling effective resonance and energy absorption. This property has led to their widespread use as a therapeutic tool in biomedical and healthcare applications. Because living organisms contain a substantial proportion of water, FIR can penetrate deeply into tissue, influencing various molecules through resonance with water molecules and modulating molecular mechanisms, thereby eliciting a range of physiological effects. The effects of FIR have been examined across diverse disciplines. The present review focuses on the effects of FIR on the nervous system. It compiles and discusses findings from previous studies that have used animal models of nervous system diseases to explore the direct effects of FIR on various aspects of the nervous system, including memory impairment, cognitive function, neural regeneration, sleep, anti-inflammatory effects, and stress relief.

papers.title: Probable Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Behavior Disorder Associated With Escitalopram in a Patient With Schizoaffective Disorder: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia in which the normal muscle atonia of REM sleep is lost, and patients act out their dreams. Serotonergic antidepressants such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are a recognized trigger, but in psychiatric patients the nocturnal behaviors are easily attributed to stress or to the primary illness. We report the case of a 46-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, maintained on aripiprazole 15 mg daily, who was started on escitalopram 10 mg at bedtime (day one); the dose was reduced to 5 mg on day 77. Around day 430, about 14 months after starting escitalopram and while taking 5 mg, he began to walk in his sleep and act out his dreams, including punching movements and, on one occasion, walking while holding a clothing iron, with no recollection on waking. The episodes occurred late in the night, with his eyes closed, two to three times a month and were accompanied by sleep paralysis and daytime sleepiness. His mental status examination and routine blood tests were unremarkable. He declined polysomnography and brain imaging, so a diagnosis of probable RBD, possibly associated with escitalopram, was made on clinical grounds; a non-REM parasomnia could not be excluded. On day 616, escitalopram was stopped and clonazepam 0.5 mg at bedtime was started at the same time. The episodes had stopped by day 665. Clonazepam was discontinued on day 772, and at the latest follow-up on day 1962 there had been no recurrence. Because clonazepam was started when escitalopram was withdrawn, the improvement cannot be attributed to stopping escitalopram alone, although the absence of recurrence after clonazepam was discontinued supports a role for the antidepressant. Clinicians who prescribe serotonergic antidepressants should take a sleep history from patients and their bed partners, arrange polysomnography where it is available, and review the suspected drug.

papers.title: Night-shift work and risk of incident musculoskeletal disorders: a prospective cohort study with proteomic mediation analysis in the UK Biobank.
papers.abstract: Night-shift work disrupts circadian rhythms and may contribute to musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs). However, large-scale prospective evidence on this association and potential biological pathways remains limited. We conducted a prospective cohort study of 179 924 employed UK Biobank participants free of MSDs at baseline and followed for a median of 13.1 years. Night-shift exposure was classified as rare, some and usual/permanent. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate HRs for incident MSDs. Proteomic analyses were performed to identify circulating proteins associated with night-shift work and MSD outcomes and to evaluate their potential mediating roles. Compared with day workers, all night-shift categories were associated with higher MSD risk: rare (HR 1.12, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.16), some (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.17) and usual/permanent (HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.20). Associations were particularly evident for osteoarthritis (HR 1.23, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.32), spinal disorders (HR 1.20, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.37) and mechanical and pain disorders of the spine (HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.42), with stronger associations among individuals with ≥10 years of exposure. Elevated risks were most pronounced in healthcare, manufacturing, tourism and cleaning sectors. Proteomic analyses identified 78 candidate mediator proteins shared across key outcomes, including apolipoprotein F, angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 and proline-rich acidic protein 1. Night-shift work was associated with increased risk of multiple MSDs, and proteomic analyses suggested potential molecular pathways linking night-shift exposure to MSD risk. These findings support the importance of circadian-friendly scheduling and targeted occupational interventions to reduce MSD burden.

papers.title: Atypical Pediatric Epilepsy: A Narrative Review of Classification, Diagnosis, and Emerging Therapeutics.
papers.abstract: Atypical pediatric epilepsies represent a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by uncommon etiologies, variable clinical presentations, and frequent resistance to standard antiseizure medications. Recent advances in classification, along with developments in genomics, neuroimaging, and autoimmune neurology, have expanded the recognized spectrum of these conditions. However, a significant proportion of children remain without a definitive syndromic diagnosis, underscoring ongoing limitations in current frameworks. This review provides a comprehensive overview of atypical epilepsy in children, including evolving classification systems, epidemiology, and etiological mechanisms spanning genetic, structural, metabolic, and immune-mediated causes. Key syndromes - including Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome, infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, and febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome - are discussed with emphasis on clinical features, differential diagnosis, and prognosis. Diagnostic challenges such as phenotypic overlap, EEG limitations, and barriers to timely genetic testing are also examined. Emerging therapeutic strategies highlight a paradigm shift from broad-spectrum seizure control toward precision medicine, including targeted pharmacologic agents, antisense oligonucleotides, gene therapies, and neuromodulation approaches. Improved recognition and classification of atypical epilepsies, coupled with early implementation of targeted therapies, are essential to optimize outcomes in this vulnerable population.

papers.title: Clinical features and long-term outcomes of anti-DPPX autoimmune encephalitis: a multicentre retrospective study in a Chinese cohort.
papers.abstract: To explore the clinical characteristics and long-term prognostic factors of anti-Dipeptidyl-peptidase-like protein 6 (DPPX) antibody encephalitis in Chinese patients. This study retrospectively included anti-DPPX antibody encephalitis patients diagnosed at three medical centres from January 2019 to May 2024. modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and Clinical Assessment Scale in Autoimmune Encephalitis (CASE) were used to evaluate baseline, short-term (3 months) and long-term (12 months) outcomes. Furthermore, we analysed the relationship between clinical characteristics, immune markers and prognosis. 15 patients were included (median age 45, 60% female). Predominant symptoms were cognitive impairment (66.7%, 10/15), seizures (53.3%, 8/15) and psychiatric symptoms (53.3%, 8/15), with a low incidence of preceding weight loss (6.7%, 1/15); 60.0% (9/15) of patients had abnormal brain MRI findings. Both mRS and CASE scores significantly improved at 3 and 12 months of follow-up (all p<0.05), but 46.2% (5/11) of patients still had memory impairment after 12 months of follow-up. Short-term disease severity (3M-CASE) was significantly positively correlated with hospital stay (β=0.22, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.42, p=0.03), psychiatric disorders (β=2.71, 95% CI 0.26 to 5.17, p=0.03), intensive care unit admission (β=4.11, 95% CI 2.07 to 6.15, p=0.001) and MRI abnormalities (β=3.13, 95% CI 0.73 to 5.52, p=0.02). Long-term disease severity (12M-CASE) was significantly correlated with sleep disorders (β=2.72, 95% CI 0.36 to 5.08, p=0.03). No specific immunological biomarkers remained significantly correlated with CASE scores after adjustment for multiple comparisons. No clinical relapse was observed in the 11 patients with available long-term follow-up data. This study delineates the clinical phenotype of anti-DPPX encephalitis in China. Immunotherapy was significantly associated with improvements in short-term and long-term outcomes. Prognostic factors and relevant immune biomarkers differ between disease stages, underscoring the need for long-term management and stage-specific immunointervention.

papers.title: Digital Health Coaching in Pregnancy: A Scoping Review of Interventions and Outcomes.
papers.abstract: Health coaching is an innovative model of health promotion, empowering individuals to enhance self-care, make informed choices, and develop health knowledge and skills. Integrating digital technologies like mobile apps, web platforms, wearables, and artificial intelligence into health coaching enables personalized, accessible, and continuous support to improve disease management. In maternal health, digital coaching promotes healthy behaviors in nutrition, physical activity, sleep, and mental well-being. This review explores digital health coaching interventions during pregnancy and their impact on maternal and fetal outcomes. We conducted a scoping review of English-language articles from 2000 until December 2024 in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE, and Google Scholar. Keywords that formed the search strategy were "digital health"," health coaching ","pregnancy" along with synonyms and related terms. Thirty- one studies were included. Most interventions used smartphones, text messaging, coaching applications, virtual sessions, and wearable devices focusing on nutrition and physical activity to manage weight and gestational diabetes. Nutritionists, obstetricians, and midwives were the main contributors, using motivational interviewing, goal setting, and social cognitive theories. Outcomes showed acceptability and satisfaction in 45% of studies, feasibility in 35%, and effectiveness in lifestyle behaviors in 68%. Improvements in weight management, glycemic control, and body composition were observed in 42% of studies.10% noted benefits in maternal and newborn health. One study reported cost-effectiveness; however, some found no significant differences in gestational weight gain or diabetes. Digital health coaching in pregnancy can have favorable potential to support mothers' health and change their behavior. However, more research is needed on the most effective components, including psychological aspects and socio-economic measures.

papers.title: Neural correlates of perceptual biases in duration perception.
papers.abstract: How we perceive a current event depends not only on its immediate context, but also on how our internal expectations are shaped by prior experience. In time perception, these expectations manifest as systematic biases, namely sequential dependence, where the current percept is influenced by the previous stimulus, and central tendency, the overestimation of short durations and underestimation of long ones. Both perceptual biases, corresponding to individual beliefs about stimulus generation, can vary substantially between participants. However, the neural responses related to inter-individual differences in these biases remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate this question in a duration reproduction task. Our EEG results show that in the frontocentral region, the Contingent Negative Variation (CNV) while experiencing the current stimulus depends on the previous stimulus regardless of sequential dependence. In contrast, in the right parietal region, the slow potential was not influenced by previous duration but associated with inter-individual differences in sequential dependence. Stimulus-offset evoked P2 amplitude was associated with both central tendency and sequential dependence and P2 amplitude varied with previous stimulus duration depending on individual sequential dependence. A Bayesian model of time perception reproduced the observed neural dynamics of the frontocentral CNV and its dependence on previous stimulus duration, suggesting that individual internal time estimates and expectations of stimulus offset are reflected in EEG responses. Our results demonstrate that both forms of perceptual bias are reflected in neural activity while experiencing the ongoing stimulus, suggesting that neural processes related to perceptual biases directly affect the measurement of time.

papers.title: Role of reverse remodelling in recurrence of atrial fibrillation after patient-tailored catheter ablation.
papers.abstract: Catheter ablation (CA) is a curative treatment for atrial fibrillation (AF), yet success rates remain sub-optimal, with ∼50% of patients with persistent AF experiencing recurrence after 1 year. This may be due to the self-perpetuating nature of AF, which remodels atrial structure and cellular properties, while successful treatment can induce reverse remodelling (RR). This study develops a patient-specific CA strategy to directly target re-entrant drivers (RDs) and investigates the role of RR in AF recurrence. Left atrial (LA) models were reconstructed from LGE-MRI scans of AF patients (n = 15) and coupled with the Courtemanche-Ramirez-Nattel (CRN) electrophysiology model. RDs were induced via pacing, identified using DGM analysis, and targeted ablation was performed in-silico. Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) was applied as a reference. Following termination, AF recurrence was tested under three levels of electrical reverse remodelling (ERR: 0%, 50%, and 100%), with and without structural reverse remodelling (SRR). Targeted ablation acutely terminated AF in all patient-specific models. After the first procedure, AF recurrence decreased progressively from 55% at 0% ERR to 36.7% at 50% ERR and 5% at 100% ERR; with additional SRR, recurrence was further reduced to 46.7%, 26.7%, and 0%, respectively. After the second CA procedure, AF recurrence rate was 42.9%, 17.9%, and 0% without SRR and 25%, 14.3%, and 0% with SRR. This study highlights the importance of RR for therapy success, with a novel targeted CA technique ensuring <5% AF recurrence in patient-specific simulations. After clinical validation, this approach can help improve long-term patient outcomes.
papers.journal: Europace : European pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac electrophysiology : journal of the working groups on cardiac pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac cellular electrophysiology of the European Society of Cardiology

papers.title: Self-Reported Cannabis Use, Pain and Mental Health in People With Inheritable Bleeding Disorders.
papers.abstract: Medical cannabis use has increased in the United States for managing symptoms such as pain, anxiety, sleep disturbance, and mood disorders. Self-report remains the primary method for documenting cannabis use. Little is known about cannabis use or perceived effectiveness among people with inheritable bleeding disorders (PWBD). Explore cannabis use patterns in PWBD who voluntarily participate in the Community Voices in Research (CVR) registry. A cross-sectional analysis was conducted using self-reported CVR data, including demographics, diagnosis, cannabis use, and pain, depression, anxiety, resiliency/coping, and social support. Of 88 participants, 25 (28.4%) stated using cannabis for symptom management. Use was reported across hemophilia A, hemophilia B, von Willebrand disease, platelet disorders, and rare bleeding disorders. There were no statistically significant differences between groups for age, birth sex, and diagnosis. Participants most commonly cited pain, anxiety, sleep, and depression as reasons for use, with the highest perceived effectiveness (0-10 scale) for sleep (8.35), anxiety (7.06), and pain (6.36). Participants who reported cannabis use demonstrated higher anxiety scores and significantly higher opioid use compared to non-cannabis users. Cannabis use was relatively common among this small sample of PWBD. These patterns may reflect gaps in care. Higher anxiety scores and opioid use among participants who reported cannabis use support the need for proactive, non-judgmental assessment and comprehensive, patient-centered symptom management strategies in this population.
papers.journal: Haemophilia : the official journal of the World Federation of Hemophilia

papers.title: The association between cardiovascular diseases and their risk factors in Austria and Slovakia: regression analyses based on the European Health Interview Survey (2019).
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) account for one in three deaths in the European Union. Slovakia has twice the rate of amenable mortality than neighboring Austria. This study aimed to examine the association between CVDs and risk factors and to describe similarities and differences in the observed patterns. Weighted 2019 European Health Interview Survey data were analyzed for adults aged ≥ 45 in Austria and Slovakia. Multivariable logistic regression analyses assessed associations between CVDs and its risk factors, adjusting for socioeconomic and demographic characteristics, and regions. The Austrian sample included 9,501 respondents and the SK sample 3,505. CVD prevalence was 8.8% in Austria and 15.3% in Slovakia. In both countries, sleep problems (Austria: OR: 1.90, 95% CI: 1.57-2.32; Slovakia: OR: 2.44, 95% CI: 1.95-3.04) were associated with reporting CVDs. In Austria, hypertension (OR: 1.88, 95% CI: 1.54-2.30), and diabetes (OR: 1.81, 95% CI: 1.42-2.31) were also associated with CVDs, as were diabetes (OR: 1.69, 95% CI: 1.31-2.20) and physical inactivity (OR: 1.65, 95% CI: 1.16-2.36) in Slovakia. Regional associations were more pronounced in Austria than in Slovakia. Although causality cannot be inferred, patterns in CVD prevalence and associated risk factors may support targeted national and regional prevention strategies.
papers.journal: Expert review of pharmacoeconomics & outcomes research

papers.title: Autonomic Reactivity and EEG-defined Clusters Reveal Distinct Chronic Pain Profiles.
papers.abstract: This study examined whether integrating stress-related heart rate variability (HRV) with resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) could characterize physiological subgroups in Chronic pain after spine surgery (CPSS). A total of 177 patients completed pain- and emotion-related questionnaires, a 3-minute resting-state EEG recording, and HRV assessments during baseline, mental arithmetic stress, and recovery. Participants were grouped by the direction of stress-related low-frequency/high-frequency (LF/HF) ratio change. Principal component analysis and unsupervised clustering were applied to 437 EEG features encompassing absolute power, cerebral asymmetry, and theta/beta ratio (TBR). After multivariate outlier detection, 168 participants underwent clustering. A 2 × 2 factorial ANOVA examined HRV-group and EEG-cluster effects on pain scores. LF/HF -decreased group (n = 56) reported higher depressive symptom scores than the increase group (n = 121, P = 0.045), without significant pain differences. Among 437 EEG features, PC1 reflected beta activity (34.39% variance), PC2 frontal/frontotemporal asymmetry (14.52%), and PC3 TBR features (9.55%). Two EEG clusters (n = 88 and n = 80) showed no significant pain- or emotion-related differences. Factorial analysis revealed nonsignificant HRV (P = .056) and EEG main effects (P = .107), but a nominally significant interaction [P = .030, partial η² = .028 (HC3-robust P = .044)]. Within EEG Cluster 0, the LF/HF-decrease group reported higher pain scores than the LF/HF-increase group (70.9 vs. 42.3; Tukey-adjusted P = .019). Integrating HRV-EEG profiles may help characterize CPSS heterogeneity. These exploratory findings, without study-wide multiplicity adjustment, require independent validation before clinical application.

Exercise and physiological monitoring in isolated, confined and extreme environments and space analogues: A scoping review.
papers.abstract: This scoping review synthesized evidence on physical activity/exercise and physiological monitoring in isolated, confined and extreme (ICE) environments, with emphasis on Antarctic missions and space analogues. ICE exposures combine cold stress, confinement, disrupted light-dark cycles and psychosocial strain, which can challenge musculoskeletal integrity, cardiovascular regulation, sleep/circadian function and cognition. Following Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidance, we searched Web of Science, Embase, Scopus and PubMed/Medline, complemented by grey literature and AI-assisted citation chasing. Eligible reports included human studies in ICE/analogue settings that implemented or quantified physical activity/exercise and/or physiological monitoring. Seventeen studies published between 2003 and 2025 met inclusion criteria and were mapped across ICE characteristics, exercise protocols, monitoring technologies, outcomes and research gaps. Exercise was reported as a potential countermeasure to attenuate selected aspects of deconditioning and support sleep and psychophysiological adaptation, particularly in bed rest and simulated confinement studies. Antarctic field studies more often characterized spontaneous physical activity, sleep/activity rhythms and field-adapted monitoring. Assessment strategies varied, ranging from self-reported logs and actigraphy in operational field settings to laboratory-grade measures in bed rest and simulated confinement studies. Overall, exercise emerged as a pragmatic, domain-specific countermeasure against deconditioning in ICE settings, with effectiveness varying by modality and physiological target. However, heterogeneity in exposure characterization, exercise dose and monitoring methods, despite feasible wearable-based capture of behavioural and physiological signals, limited comparability and mechanistic inference. Future ICE research should prioritize harmonized reporting, standardized monitoring and longitudinal designs linking exercise exposure to physiological, behavioural and operational outcomes.

papers.title: Comparing two wrist-worn accelerometers (Axivity AX3 and Matrix 003) for measuring movement behaviours in British and Chinese older adults.
papers.abstract: Two nationally representative cohorts, the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), recently introduced accelerometry to measure movement behaviours. However, the use of different brands (Axivity AX3 and Matrix 003) may hinder data harmonisation. This study assessed whether the raw acceleration data and machine learning-derived physical activity and sleep outcomes were equivalent between these two accelerometers in both British and Chinese adults. Eighty-five British and 117 Chinese adults aged ≥50 years wore both accelerometers in a random order on their dominant wrist for up to eight days. Data were processed using UK-derived machine learning algorithms to generate outcomes such as average acceleration (mg), time in 24-hour movement behaviours (hours/day), daily step count, and sleep duration (hours/night). Equivalency was assessed using 95% equivalence tests (±10% equivalence zone). In both British and Chinese adults, average acceleration, sedentary time, time in bed, and sleep duration were equivalent between the two accelerometers, while time in moderate-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) was not (±17.7% in British and ±28.2% in Chinese adults). Time in light physical activity (LPA) was equivalent in British (±6.2%) but borderline in Chinese adults (±10.3%), whereas the opposite was observed for daily step count (±10.5% in British and ±2.9% in Chinese adults). Average acceleration was comparable between the Axivity AX3 and the Matrix 003 in both British and Chinese adults. Machine learning-derived outcomes were also largely comparable; however, the cross-nationality differences highlight the need for further population-specific algorithm development and validation.
